10 Best Buster Keaton Movies

Featured | List
By:Shaswata Ray Updated:August 26, 2026

“Deadpan and Dangerous”

Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 17:09
Instaread

There’s a particular kind of magic to watching a Buster Keaton film for the first time. You brace yourself for something creaky and antique, the way silent comedy sometimes gets stereotyped, and instead you get a guy calmly getting flattened by a house, riding a motorcycle he doesn’t realise has no driver, or hanging off a moving train by one hand — and never once cracking a smile while doing it. A hundred years later, none of it has lost its nerve.

Keaton was born in 1895 into a vaudeville family, and by age three he was already part of his parents’ rough-and-tumble stage act. That early training built the foundation for everything that came after: the total physical fearlessness, the instinct for timing, and that famously unreadable face that earned him the nickname “The Great Stone Face.” With his own production unit, until around 1928, Keaton ran through one of the most astonishing creative streaks in film history. First he had a run of tightly built two-reel shorts, then a string of features he wrote, directed, produced, and starred in, often performing stunts that could have genuinely killed him if his timing had been off by inches.

That run ended, more or less, when he signed with MGM in 1928. The studio system stripped away the creative control that had made his best work possible, and Keaton spent much of the following decade fighting alcoholism and watching his career shrink to gag-writing gigs and bit parts. Later in life, however, Keaton lived to see his silent work rediscovered and reappraised by a new generation of critics and filmmakers, and today he’s spoken of in the same breath as Chaplin. The following ten films, in our judgement, represent Keaton at his sharpest.

10. The Navigator (1924)

Rollo Treadway (Buster Keaton) proposes marriage to his neighbour Betsy (Kathryn McGuire) one fine morning, even booking a honeymoon trip to Honolulu, only to be flatly rejected. Following a tangle of coincidences and one badly misread pier number, the two of them nevertheless end up alone aboard ‘The Navigator’ – a massive ocean liner drifting across the Pacific after being cut loose from its moorings.

This sets the stage for a series of experiments in incompetence as Rollo and Betsy, both having grown up rich and pampered, struggle to take care of themselves, left to their own devices. The ship itself becomes something of an antagonist in the film, its scale dwarfing the humans stumbling around its deck, and Keaton obtains remarkable comic mileage by juxtaposing the liner’s industrial enormity and the smallness of the fundamental domestic tasks his characters are failing at.

Complete with an underwater sequence in which Rollo, in a full diving suit, fends off a swordfish, the film formally has Keaton working closer to survivalist fantasy. Thematically, it inverts the millionaire-toughened-by-adversity arc he’d use elsewhere: here the point isn’t transformation so much as endurance, as two spoiled people discover a scrappy competence between themselves they never imagined they had. Kathryn McGuire also deserves credit here – she’s given actual stuff to do rather than just standing around looking pretty, which wasn’t always true for women in silent films.

9. Go West (1925)

At number nine, we’ve got the sweetest film on this list, and also maybe the strangest: a Buster Keaton movie where the love interest is a cow. Keaton plays a drifter named Friendless, who’s got nothing and nobody except a photo of his mother and a few coins in his pocket when he decides to “Go West” and try his luck. He ends up accidentally at a struggling Arizona cattle ranch owned by Mr Thompson (Howard Truesdale), whose daughter (Kathleen Myers) and ranch foreman (Ray Thompson) watch this hopeless city kid try to figure out which end of a cow is which. He’s terrible at ranch work. Genuinely, comically terrible, with a whole bit where he tries to milk a cow by just sticking a bucket underneath her and waiting.

But Friendless does find one friend: a cow named Brown Eyes, who’s about to be culled from the herd for not producing milk. Something about her sad outcast energy matches Friendless’s own, and the two become inseparable. It’s a genuinely tender relationship, and Keaton plays it completely straight, no winking at the camera about the ridiculousness of his best mate being livestock. Unlike most of Keaton’s more famous works, there isn’t as much death-defying stunt work, but a lot more heart. This is a movie about a guy who’s never had anything or anyone close enough to protect, finally finding something worth protecting, even if it’s just a cow.

8. Three Ages (1923)

Keaton’s first solo feature, the first that he wrote, directed, produced, and also starred in, follows his character (called only The Boy) competing for the same woman (Margaret Leahy, in her only film role) against the same brutish rival (Wallace Beery), and it does this across the Stone Age, ancient Rome, and 1920s America, cutting back and forth between all three. It’s considered to be a gentle spoof of D.W. Griffith‘s “Intolerance” (1926), which had done something similar, albeit far more self-serious, just a few years earlier. The joke, more or less, seems to be that romantic rivalry looks exactly the same whether you’re swinging a club or driving a car.

Each segment has its own flavour of gag. In the Stone Age bit, Keaton and Beery settle their rivalry with a round of golf played with actual boulders, with a bizarrely charming scene involving a turtle used as something like a makeshift Ouija board. The Roman section escalates things into a chariot race, except Keaton’s chariot is pulled by a pack of dogs instead of horses.

And the modern-day thread drops Keaton into 1920s traffic and technology, sputtering along in a car that displays active hostility towards him. What’s most interesting about “Three Ages,” more than a 100 years later, isn’t really the intentionally thin plot but rather watching Keaton work out his directorial instincts: trying on different historical textures, testing how far a single repeated joke could be stretched across genre and setting.

7. Battling Butler (1926)

A film that’s easily overlooked despite Keaton himself considering it his personal favourite, Battling Butler’s climactic boxing scene was realistic enough to inspire Scorsese’s staging in “Raging Bull.” Alfred Butler (Buster Keaton), a millionaire’s son, lives such a pampered life that his valet remains on hand to flick off his cigarette ashes.

Out on a hunting trip, Alfred falls for a mountain girl (Sally O’Neil), only to be met with her father and brother’s disapproval. His valet, however, saves the day by seizing on a coincidence: there’s a real professional boxer making headlines under the exact same name, Alfred “Battling” Butler (Francis McDonald). While the masquerade buys our Alfred some respect, it also traps him in a deception that keeps getting more complex.

The film is striking in how patiently it builds, with Keaton’s face (as blank and unreadable as ever) doing the work of showing a man who has never once been asked to notice the world around him. It becomes something of a suspense-comedy once the mistaken-identity plot kicks in, with each subsequent complication raising the stakes around Alfred’s lie rather than merely setting up the next gag. “Battling Butler” presents a variation on one of Keaton’s favourite subjects – where the useless man is forced to acquire capability. But unlike other Keaton protagonists outdone by machines or nature, Alfred is outmatched by the softness he inherits, and the film asks whether that kind of transformation can ever be more than mere appearance.

6. Seven Chances (1925)

“Seven Chances” has one of the most gloriously foolish premises Keaton ever worked with, yet he somehow still makes it work. Jimmy Shannon (Buster Keaton) is a young broker whose firm is about to go under when his lawyer (Snitz Edwards) shows up with a lifeline: Jimmy stands to inherit seven million dollars, but only if he’s married by seven o’clock that same evening (his twenty-seventh birthday, as luck would have it). He rushes to propose to Mary Jones (Ruth Dwyer), the woman he’s actually loved for ages, botches it badly enough for her to turn him down, and suddenly finds himself proposing to basically any woman who’ll stand still long enough to hear the offer, while his business partner Billy Meekin (T. Roy Barnes) eggs him on.

The film’s first half keeps things relatively low-key, featuring a lovely sequence with Snitz Edwards’s spectacles coming on and off his face, as the will gets read and the number keeps climbing past their limits of incredulity. It’s small, exact, and very funny in a way that doesn’t need to announce itself. Then the film changes gears entirely as Billy plants a newspaper ad out of desperation, asking any willing bride to meet Jimmy at a church.

Jimmy, however, has to make a run for it when a small army of women in wedding dresses turn up to collect on that ad. The film’s most famous image, where Keaton sprints downhill just ahead of an avalanche of boulders, was not even pre-planned. As he describes in his autobiography, Keaton had dislodged one rock by accident during filming, and it knocked a couple more loose, and the gag landed so well in a test screening that Keaton went back and built the whole sequence around it.

5. Our Hospitality (1923)

“Our Hospitality” is one of the first films where we really see Keaton the storyteller and Keaton the daredevil start working in sync. It opens with a prologue set in 1810, showing the origins of a blood feud between the McKay and Canfield families. After his father is killed, baby Willie McKay (played by Keaton’s own infant son) is spirited off to New York to grow up far from the violence, ignorant of the whole thing. Twenty years later, Willie (now played by Buster Keaton) heads back south to claim his family’s estate, riding a rickety early steam train called the Rocket. On his journey, he meets and falls for Virginia (Natalie Talmadge, Keaton’s real-life wife at the time), a young woman with no idea that she’s a Canfield and that her family is still very much baying for McKay blood.

The only thing standing between Willie and a bullet is an old code of Southern hospitality: the Canfields simply cannot shoot a guest under their own roof. Once he catches on, Willie thus becomes almost pathologically committed to never leaving the house, producing some of the funniest situational comedy of Keaton’s career. One thing that sets apart “Our Hospitality” from the rest of Keaton’s filmography is just how seriously it takes its own period setting. The train sequence alone is a small marvel of production design, and the film shows early signs of the tonal balancing act that Keaton goes on to perfect a few years later with “The General.”

4. Steamboat Bill Jr. (1928)

A film of coherent chaos where Keaton nearly got himself killed for a single shot. William Canfield Jr. (Buster Keaton) arrives in the little river town of River Junction at his mother’s request to meet a father (Ernest Torrence) he hasn’t seen since he was small. What William “Steamboat Bill” Canfield gets back is a bow-tied college kid with a pencil moustache and a ukulele, who is nothing like the rugged riverboat captain he was hoping for.

The disappointment on Torrence’s face makes for one of the film’s quietly running gags. To add insult to injury, Bill Sr.’s steamboat business is being run to the ground by his rival, the wealthy J.J. King, whose sleek new boat makes Bill’s old Stonewall Jackson look like scrap. Complicating matters further, in typical Keaton fashion, Bill Jr. falls in love with King’s daughter Kitty (Marion Byron).

“Steamboat Bill Jr.“ extracts a lot of comic value out of the sheer physical mismatch between Torrence and Keaton, the former towering over the latter by nearly a foot. There’s a terrific scene where the father drags his son around town trying to dress him into looking more like a man, holding up hat after hat with growing despair. Keaton had originally planned to end the film with a flood, but real flooding along the Mississippi during production forced a rewrite. So Keaton pivoted to a cyclone instead and built some of the most jaw-dropping sequences in silent film. In the single most famous image of Keaton’s career, the entire two-ton facade of a house collapses directly onto him, an open window frame the only thing standing between him and serious injury.

3. The Cameraman (1928)

Buster (Buster Keaton) makes his living as a street photographer, snapping cheap tintype portraits of passersby for pocket change. When a crowd of press photographers swarms past him chasing some visiting dignitary, he gets jostled up against a young woman named Sally (Marceline Day) and falls for her instantly. She barely notices him. But he tracks her down to her job as a secretary at MGM’s newsreel department, and decides that the fastest way into her orbit is to become a newsreel cameraman himself. There’s just one problem: he’s never operated a movie camera in his life, and the second-hand one he scrapes together his savings to buy starts falling apart before he’s even shot a frame.

What follows is Keaton charting just how bad someone can be at a job while still refusing to quit, in painfully funny detail. His early footage comes back as double exposures and total nonsense, the kind of thing that gets him laughed out of the newsroom. There’s a wonderfully cramped little sequence where he ends up sharing a single changing room with another man at a public pool, and the two of them get so tangled up swapping in and out of the same undersized space that it becomes its own miniature ballet of frustration. But “The Cameraman” transcends being a mere string of gags by being a movie about filmmaking itself, and about the gap between what a camera captures and what actually happens.

2. The General (1926)

Second on this list and, for most critics and historians, widely considered Keaton’s magnum opus and one of the greatest films of the silent era. Johnnie Gray (Buster Keaton) has two loves in his life: his locomotive, a beauty named ‘The General’, and a young woman named Annabelle Lee (Marion Mack). When the Civil War breaks out, and Johnnie rushes to enlist, he’s turned away not because anyone doubts his nerve, but because the Confederate Army decides he’s worth more to them as an engineer than behind a rifle. However, nobody bothers explaining that to Annabelle, and she and her family write him off as a coward, refusing to so much as speak to him until he’s in uniform.

A year passes, and then Union spies steal The General with Annabelle unknowingly still aboard. Johnnie takes off after his train alone, commandeering a second locomotive called the Texas, and what follows is one of the greatest chase sequences ever put on film, silent or otherwise. Keaton insisted on using full-sized functioning locomotives rather than models, shot much of it on real Oregon track, and staged a train wreck so massive and expensive that it reportedly remains one of the more costly single shots of the entire silent era.

1. Sherlock Jr. (1924)

In this delightful little film, Keaton plays a small-town movie theatre projectionist, the kind of guy who’s teaching himself detective work from a how-to manual in his spare time while barely scraping by. He’s got his eye on a girl (Kathryn McGuire), but competition shows up in the form of a local rival (Ward Crane), who frames him for stealing her father’s pocket watch to get him out of the picture. Humiliated and shut out of the girl’s house, our projectionist trudges back to work, slumps into his booth, and falls asleep mid-screening.

This is when the film does something genuinely startling for 1924: his dreaming self gets up, walks down the theatre aisle, and steps directly into the movie playing on the screen. Keaton becomes the movie’s dashing detective hero “Sherlock Jr.,” and for a few glorious minutes the film-within-the-film keeps cutting the ground out from under him. He’s diving off a rock one second and landing face-first in a snowbank the next, the location changing out from under him before he can adjust –  a man rudely discovering that he doesn’t control the editing of his own dream.

There’s the moment Keaton perches on the handlebars of a motorcycle with no idea the driver’s already fallen off, and rides it unassisted through traffic, across a gap in a bridge, and past oncoming trains. “Sherlock Jr.” elevates itself above mere spectacle by being tightly constructed around the idea of movies themselves: how they shape what we wish we could be, and how badly that wish can fail to translate back into real life.
